title: Thyroid examination in a 32-year-old woman with a neck swelling
desc: This station involves a short focused history and a full thyroid examination of a 32-year-old accountant who has a neck swelling, weight loss and an irregular pulse. The candidate then interprets her thyroid function tests and antibodies, ECG and baseline bloods, makes the diagnosis, and plans rate control, antithyroid treatment, anticoagulation assessment, referrals and safety netting in general practice.
focus: Systematic thyroid status and goitre examination: recognising Graves' disease with orbitopathy and thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation, and starting safe management in general practice
stem: You are a GP registrar in a suburban general practice. Eliza, a 32-year-old accountant, has made an appointment because of a swelling in her neck.
tasks: Take a focused history from Eliza and perform a focused thyroid examination, telling the examiner what you are examining (10 minutes).

The examiner will give you Eliza's thyroid function tests and thyroid antibodies, her ECG and her baseline blood tests. Interpret them, then outline your management approach and safety netting (5 minutes).
patient:
Role: You are Eliza, a 32-year-old accountant. You are a bit restless and fidgety, talk quickly, and are keen to get back to work. You are cooperative and agree to be examined, sitting on a chair with your neck and arms exposed. Do not volunteer details: give each answer only when asked. The examiner gives the examination findings below when the candidate says what they would examine.

Opening line: "A colleague told me my neck looks swollen, and now I can see it in the mirror too."

The neck swelling (give only when asked):

  • First noticed by a colleague about 2 months ago; it seems to have slowly got bigger.
  • It is not painful or tender. No recent sore throat, cold or flu.
  • No trouble swallowing, no breathlessness lying flat, no noisy breathing and no change in your voice.

Other symptoms (give each only when asked about it):

  • Weight: you have lost about 6 kg in 3 months (62 kg down to 56 kg) without trying, even though you are eating more than usual.
  • Heat: you feel hot when others are comfortable and sweat a lot; you sleep with the window open.
  • Heart: for about 3 weeks your heart has felt like it is "fluttering and racing, all over the place", on and off, worse when you lie down at night. No chest pain, no breathlessness, no fainting or near-fainting, no ankle swelling.
  • Nerves and sleep: shaky hands (your handwriting is messier), anxious and irritable, sleeping badly. Your partner says you "can't sit still".
  • Bowels: opening your bowels 2 or 3 times a day, softer than usual. No blood.
  • Periods: lighter and coming every 6 or 7 weeks for the last few months. Last period started 3 weeks ago.
  • Eyes: they feel gritty and water in the wind, and friends say you look like you are "staring". No double vision, no blurred vision, no eye pain, colours look normal, and you can close your eyes fully.
  • Muscles: a bit tired climbing the stairs at work, but you manage.

Things that point away from other causes (if asked): no recent pregnancy or breastfeeding. No neck pain or fever. You take no thyroid tablets, no amiodarone, no kelp, iodine or "metabolism" or weight-loss supplements. No previous thyroid problems, neck surgery or radiation. No X-ray contrast scans recently.

Contraception and pregnancy: you and your partner use condoms. You are not trying to get pregnant now, but you would like children in the next couple of years.

Past medical history: nil. No asthma. Medicines: none. Allergies: none.

Family history: your mother has an underactive thyroid and takes thyroxine. Your aunt has type 1 diabetes.

Social history: you live with your partner. You work long hours as an accountant and it is a busy time of year. You smoke about 10 cigarettes a day and have done since university. Alcohol: about 4 to 6 standard drinks a week. Three coffees a day.

Ideas, concerns, expectations:

  • Idea: you put the weight loss and racing heart down to stress and coffee.
  • Concern: that the lump could be cancer, and that your eyes look odd in client meetings.
  • Expectation: a blood test, and to find out whether it is serious.

Question to raise in Part 1: "Could this lump be cancer?"

Exam findings (examiner: give only when the candidate says what they examine):

  • General inspection: thin, restless and fidgety. Wearing a light singlet on a cool day when others are in jumpers. Weight 56 kg, height 168 cm, BMI 19.8 kg/m². Not short of breath at rest.
  • Vital signs (give as stated): BP 130/85 mmHg. HR 105/min, irregularly irregular. RR 18/min. Temperature 37.0 °C. SpO2 98% on room air (if asked).
  • Hands: warm and moist (sweaty). Mild palmar erythema. Onycholysis of both ring fingernails. No clubbing or thyroid acropachy. No palmar crease pallor. Nails not brittle.
  • Arms: fine tremor with the arms outstretched (a sheet of paper on the hands trembles). Biceps and supinator reflexes brisk. Pemberton's sign negative (no facial plethora or distress with arms raised).
  • Face and eyes:
    • Bilateral exophthalmos: sclera visible below the iris, and the eyes protrude beyond the brow when viewed from above and from the side.
    • Lid retraction (sclera visible above the iris) with a staring look. Lid lag present on following a finger downwards.
    • Mild redness of the conjunctivae. No chemosis. Eyes close fully.
    • Eye movements full in all directions on the H test, with no double vision and no pain on movement.
    • If asked: visual acuity 6/6 in each eye; colour vision normal.
    • No conjunctival pallor. Outer eyebrows and scalp hair normal.
  • Neck, inspection: a visible, diffuse, symmetrical swelling in the anterior neck, about two to three times normal size. No scars, redness or distended veins. It moves up when she swallows a sip of water. It does not move on tongue protrusion.
  • Neck, palpation (from the front and from behind): both lobes and the isthmus are diffusely and symmetrically enlarged, smooth, soft to firm and non-tender, with no discrete nodule. The lower border is felt on swallowing. Trachea central. No cervical lymphadenopathy.
  • Percussion over the manubrium: resonant (no retrosternal extension).
  • Auscultation of the thyroid: a soft bruit over both lobes.
  • Heart and chest (if examined): heart sounds dual and irregular, no murmur. JVP not raised. Chest clear.
  • Legs: no pretibial myxoedema. No ankle oedema. Stands from a chair with arms folded, a little slowly but without help. Ankle and knee reflexes brisk.

check.x: Professionalism
Hand hygiene, introduction and role, confirms Eliza's identity, explains the examination and gains consent; positions her seated with the neck and arms exposed and a glass of water ready.

Uses plain language, responds to her worry about cancer without false reassurance (a smooth diffuse goitre with no nodule is unlikely to be cancer, the tests will confirm the cause), and acknowledges her embarrassment about her eyes.
History

Characterises the neck swelling: onset and growth (noticed 2 months ago, slowly enlarging), pain or tenderness (none), and pressure symptoms: trouble swallowing, breathlessness or stridor, hoarse voice (none).
Asks about symptoms of thyrotoxicosis:
check.d: Award when at least two of the three kids are covered.

kids.x: Weight loss despite a good appetite (6 kg in 3 months), heat intolerance and sweating.
Palpitations (irregular, racing, for 3 weeks), tremor, anxiety, irritability and poor sleep.
Frequent bowel motions and lighter, less frequent periods.

check.x: Asks about eye symptoms: grittiness, watering, staring appearance (present), and specifically double vision, blurred or reduced vision, altered colour vision and eye pain (none).
Screens for cardiac complications of the palpitations: chest pain, breathlessness, fainting or near-fainting, ankle swelling (none).

Asks about other causes, past history including asthma, medicines and family history: neck pain or recent viral illness, recent pregnancy, thyroxine, amiodarone, iodine or kelp supplements, recent contrast, previous thyroid disease (none); no asthma (relevant to beta blockers), no medicines or allergies; mother hypothyroid on thyroxine, aunt with type 1 diabetes.
check.d: Award when the candidate asks about medicines or supplements (including thyroxine, amiodarone or iodine), asthma, and family history of thyroid or autoimmune disease. Credit, but do not require: neck pain or recent viral illness, recent pregnancy, recent contrast, previous thyroid disease, allergies. Credit, but do not require: last period, contraception and pregnancy plans (condoms; would like children in the next couple of years). Contraception is scored again in Part 2.

check.x: Takes a social history: smoking quantified (10 a day), alcohol and caffeine, work stress.
Explores ideas, concerns and expectations: thinks it is stress and coffee, worried about cancer and her eyes, expects a blood test.
Examination

General inspection (thin, restless, lightly dressed for the weather) and asks for vital signs and weight, noting the irregularly irregular pulse [BP 130/85, HR 105 irregular, RR 18, temperature 37.0 °C, weight 56 kg].
Examines the hands: temperature and sweating, palmar erythema, onycholysis, acropachy or clubbing [warm, moist, palmar erythema, onycholysis; no acropachy].
check.d: Credit, but do not require: palmar crease pallor [none].

check.x: Tests for a fine tremor with the arms outstretched, tests reflexes for briskness, and performs Pemberton's sign [fine tremor, brisk reflexes, Pemberton's negative].
Examines the eyes for thyroid eye disease:
check.d: Award when all three kids are done. Credit, but do not require: visual acuity and colour vision [6/6, normal]; chemosis [none]; outer eyebrows [normal].

kids.x: Inspects from the front, the side and above for exophthalmos [present on both sides].
Looks for lid retraction and tests for lid lag [both present].
Tests eye movements with an H pattern, asking about double vision or pain [full, no diplopia].

check.x: Inspects the neck from the front for a goitre, scars, redness and distended veins, then with a sip of water and with tongue protrusion [diffuse goitre, rises on swallowing, not on tongue protrusion].

Palpates from behind (and the front), describing size, symmetry, consistency, tenderness, nodules and the lower border on swallowing, and checks the cervical nodes and trachea [diffuse, smooth, soft-firm, non-tender, no nodule; nodes none; trachea central].
Percusses over the manubrium for retrosternal extension and auscultates the thyroid for a bruit [resonant; bruit over both lobes].

Examines the legs for pretibial myxoedema and proximal myopathy (stand from a chair with arms folded), and looks for signs of heart failure [none; rises without help; JVP not raised, chest clear, no oedema].
Interpretation

Thyroid function: suppressed TSH (below 0.01) with high free T4 (48) and free T3 (18.5) is overt thyrotoxicosis that is not TSH-driven (not pituitary, where TSH would be normal or high); the cause is then shown by the antibodies and clinical features.
check.d: Accept "TSH-independent" or "primary" thyrotoxicosis; naming the pituitary is credit only.

check.x: Antibodies: positive TSH receptor antibodies (TRAb 12.4) confirm Graves' disease.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: positive anti-TPO supports autoimmune thyroid disease but is not specific.

check.x: ECG: atrial fibrillation (irregularly irregular, no P waves) with a ventricular rate of about 110/min and no ischaemic changes.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: narrow QRS, normal axis, normal QTc, no pre-excitation.

check.x: Baseline bloods: normal neutrophil count and liver function before an antithyroid drug, normal renal function and electrolytes, and a negative pregnancy test.
Gives the diagnosis as Graves' disease with thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation and Graves' orbitopathy, citing the diffuse goitre with bruit, eye signs, thyrotoxic features and positive TRAb.

Names at least three other causes of thyrotoxicosis, each with a feature against it here: toxic multinodular goitre, toxic adenoma, thyroiditis (subacute, painless or postpartum), exogenous thyroxine, amiodarone or iodine excess.
Management
Starts a beta blocker for symptoms and rate control after confirming no asthma (e.g. propranolol 10 to 40 mg orally three or four times daily, or metoprolol).
check.d: Credit, but do not require: a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker (verapamil or diltiazem) if a beta blocker is contraindicated.

check.x: Assesses stroke risk with CHA2DS2-VA (score 0, so anticoagulation is not recommended now; reassess if AF persists or risk factors change).
check.d: Accept CHA2DS2-VASc 1 from female sex alone with the same conclusion. Credit, but do not require: echocardiogram; AF usually reverts once euthyroid, so cardioversion is deferred (with anticoagulation around any planned cardioversion).

check.x: Starts carbimazole (commonly 15 to 30 mg daily) after discussion with endocrinology, or arranges it at an endocrinology review within days.
check.d: Doses need not be exact. Credit, but do not require: free T4 and T3 every 4 to 6 weeks because TSH stays suppressed for months; titrated over a 12 to 18 month course.

check.x: Names the definitive options for relapse or by choice: radioiodine (can worsen eye disease, especially in smokers) or total thyroidectomy, both usually leading to lifelong thyroxine.
check.d: Award in Q3 or Q4 (usually when answering Eliza's questions about lifelong tablets and pregnancy).

check.x: Refers urgently to endocrinology, and to ophthalmology (routine/soon for mild orbitopathy), with lubricating eye drops.
check.d: Credit, but do not require: sunglasses, sleeping head-up, selenium on specialist advice.

check.x: Advises and supports stopping smoking because it worsens eye disease (e.g. Quitline 13 78 48, nicotine replacement).
Advises reliable contraception while on carbimazole and planning any pregnancy with endocrinology.
check.d: Award in Q3 or Q4 (usually when answering Eliza's questions about lifelong tablets and pregnancy). Credit, but do not require: propylthiouracil in the first trimester; no pregnancy for 6 months after radioiodine.

check.x: Safety netting
Warns about agranulocytosis on carbimazole: if she gets a sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers, stop the tablet and have an urgent full blood count the same day (GP or ED).
Tells her to call 000 or go to ED for chest pain, breathlessness, fainting or a very fast heartbeat, or fever with confusion or vomiting (possible thyroid storm).
check.d: Award when the candidate names at least two cardiac red flags (chest pain, breathlessness, fainting, very fast heartbeat) and at least one thyroid storm feature (fever with confusion, agitation or vomiting), with 000 or ED. Credit, but do not require: stroke symptoms.

check.x: Tells her that blurred or reduced vision, colours looking washed out, double vision or painful eyes need same-day eye review or ED.
Arranges GP review within about a week and thyroid function tests in 4 to 6 weeks.
check.d: Award in Q3 or Q4. Credit, but do not require: specialist appointments confirmed, written information.

part2.lead: During the consultation the practice nurse recorded an ECG; Eliza was haemodynamically stable and you sent urgent bloods. The laboratory phoned the results through the next morning and Eliza has come back in. Here are the ECG and her results.
part2.patient:
Eliza is not part of Questions 1 to 3. She is back in the room for Question 4 and asks these while the candidate explains:

  • "Will I need to take tablets forever?"
  • "We want to have a baby in a couple of years. Is that still possible?"

Be relieved that it is not cancer. If smoking is raised, say: "I didn't know it affected my eyes. I'll give quitting a go."

handover.label: Thyroid function tests and thyroid antibodies
handover.result: Phoned through urgently by the laboratory as markedly abnormal.
handover.model:
Read: TSH below 0.01 mIU/L (suppressed) with free T4 48 pmol/L and free T3 18.5 pmol/L (both well above range): overt thyrotoxicosis. TRAb 12.4 IU/L is strongly positive; anti-TPO is also positive.

For Eliza: a suppressed TSH with high thyroid hormones means the excess hormone is not TSH-driven, so the problem is not the pituitary (which would give a normal or high TSH); positive TRAb then shows the gland is being stimulated to overproduce (Graves'), rather than leaking hormone (thyroiditis) or hormone being taken in tablets. This fits her diffuse goitre with a bruit, exophthalmos and lid retraction. Anti-TPO is common in Graves' but not specific.

What it changes: no nuclear scan is needed to find the cause. Start a beta blocker and an antithyroid drug, refer to endocrinology, and monitor free T4 and T3 rather than TSH early on.

handover.label: 12-lead ECG
handover.result:
12-lead ECG, 25 mm/s, 10 mm/mV, recorded in the practice. Eliza, 32, palpitations, irregular pulse.

  • Rate: ventricular rate about 110/min (range 90 to 130).
  • Rhythm: irregularly irregular. No discernible P waves; fine fibrillatory baseline in V1 and II.
  • Axis: normal (+60°).
  • PR: not measurable.
  • QRS: 84 ms, normal morphology. No delta wave. No voltage criteria for left ventricular hypertrophy.
  • QTc: 428 ms.
  • ST and T: no ST elevation or depression; T waves normal.
  • Comparison: no previous ECG available.

Conclusion: atrial fibrillation with a ventricular rate of about 110/min; no ischaemic changes.
handover.model:
Read: irregularly irregular narrow-complex rhythm with no P waves and a fibrillatory baseline at about 110/min: atrial fibrillation with a moderately fast ventricular rate. Normal axis, QRS and QTc, no pre-excitation, no ST or T changes, no LVH. No old ECG to compare.

For Eliza: new AF in a young woman with no heart disease is most likely caused by her thyrotoxicosis and explains her irregular racing palpitations. She is haemodynamically stable with no chest pain, breathlessness or signs of heart failure, so this can be managed outside hospital.

What it changes: rate control with a beta blocker; CHA2DS2-VA is 0, so no anticoagulation now; echocardiogram; expect reversion once euthyroid, and defer cardioversion until then; repeat the ECG at review.

handover.label: Baseline blood tests
handover.model:
Read: normal haemoglobin, white cells, neutrophils (3.2) and platelets. Normal electrolytes and kidney function (eGFR above 90). Normal liver function and calcium. Serum beta-hCG below 5 IU/L: not pregnant.

For Eliza: these are the baselines needed before an antithyroid drug, because carbimazole can rarely cause agranulocytosis or liver injury, and they let a later sore throat or jaundice be judged against a normal start. The negative pregnancy test matters because carbimazole harms the baby in early pregnancy and radioiodine is contraindicated in pregnancy.

What it changes: it is safe to start carbimazole; normal kidney function would allow any anticoagulant later if needed. Advise reliable contraception.

ask: You are now calling the endocrinology registrar at the local hospital. Please give an ISBAR handover of Eliza, including your interpretation of these results.
What is your most likely diagnosis, and what else would you consider? Justify your answer.
Outline your management of Eliza now, here in general practice.
Eliza is back in the room. Before she goes home, explain her diagnosis and treatment, answer her questions, and tell her what to watch for and what follow-up you will arrange.
expect:
• Identify: self, GP registrar; Eliza, 32, accountant.
  • Situation: new thyrotoxicosis from Graves' disease with new atrial fibrillation, haemodynamically stable. Requesting urgent review and advice on starting carbimazole.
  • Background: 2 months of painless goitre, 6 kg weight loss, heat intolerance, tremor, 3 weeks of irregular palpitations. Diffuse goitre with bruit, exophthalmos, lid retraction, no diplopia; acuity and colour vision normal if tested. Smoker 10 a day, no asthma, no medicines.
  • Assessment: TSH suppressed, fT4 48, fT3 18.5 = overt TSH-independent thyrotoxicosis; TRAb positive = Graves' hyperthyroidism. ECG: AF about 110/min, no ischaemia. Baseline FBC, LFTs, UEC normal; beta-hCG negative. CHA2DS2-VA 0.
  • Recommendation: beta blocker started; agree carbimazole dose; urgent endocrinology clinic; ophthalmology referral; echo.

Most likely: Graves' disease with thyrotoxic AF and orbitopathy. Diffuse smooth goitre with bruit, exophthalmos and lid retraction, positive TRAb, suppressed TSH with high fT4 and fT3.

  • Toxic multinodular goitre: against: young, smooth diffuse gland with no nodules, eye signs.
  • Toxic adenoma: against: no solitary nodule.
  • Thyroiditis (subacute, painless, postpartum): against: painless, afebrile, no viral illness or recent pregnancy, bruit, TRAb positive.
  • Exogenous thyroxine, amiodarone or iodine: against: no medicines or supplements, goitre present.
  • Impending thyroid storm (must not miss): against: afebrile, alert, no vomiting, no heart failure, haemodynamically stable. Admit if fever, confusion, vomiting, worsening tachycardia or heart failure develop.

1. Rate and symptom control: beta blocker (no asthma), e.g. propranolol 10 to 40 mg three or four times daily or metoprolol.
  2. AF: CHA2DS2-VA 0, so no anticoagulation now; echocardiogram; expect reversion when euthyroid; defer cardioversion.
  3. Antithyroid drug: carbimazole after discussion with endocrinology (commonly 15 to 30 mg daily); fT4 and fT3 every 4 to 6 weeks; 12 to 18 month course.
  4. Referrals: urgent endocrinology; ophthalmology; eye lubricants.
  5. Smoking cessation (worsens eye disease; Quitline).
  6. ED if unstable, chest pain, heart failure or features of thyroid storm.
  7. GP review in a week; fT4/fT3 in 4 to 6 weeks.

• Explanation: immune system overstimulating the thyroid; not cancer; tablets 12 to 18 months, and if it comes back, radioiodine or surgery with lifelong thyroxine.
  • Pregnancy: yes, but plan it with the specialist; use contraception on carbimazole.
  • Sore throat, fever, mouth ulcers: stop the tablet, same-day blood count.
  • 000 or ED: chest pain, breathlessness, fainting, very fast heart, fever with confusion or vomiting, stroke symptoms.
  • Same-day eye review: blurred vision, washed-out colours, double vision, eye pain.
  • Follow-up: as arranged (GP 1 week, TFTs 4 to 6 weeks).

ddx.dx: Graves' disease with thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation and Graves' orbitopathy
ddx.for: Diffuse smooth goitre with a bruit, exophthalmos and lid retraction, weight loss, tremor, warm moist hands, AF, suppressed TSH with high free T4 and T3, and positive TRAb.
She has a goitre with TSH-independent thyrotoxicosis.
ddx.against: She is 32, the gland is smooth and diffuse with no nodules, she has eye signs, and TRAb is positive.

ddx.for: TSH-independent thyrotoxicosis with a palpable thyroid.
ddx.against: There is no solitary nodule, both lobes are enlarged, and TRAb is positive.

ddx.for: Thyrotoxicosis with a goitre in a young woman.
ddx.against: The gland is non-tender, she is afebrile with no viral illness or recent pregnancy, there is a bruit (increased blood flow), eye disease and positive TRAb.

ddx.dx: Exogenous thyroid hormone, amiodarone or iodine excess
ddx.for: Thyrotoxicosis in a young woman; weight-loss or 'metabolism' supplements can contain thyroid hormone or iodine.
ddx.against: She takes no medicines or supplements, and she has a goitre with eye signs and positive TRAb.

ddx.for: Severe biochemical thyrotoxicosis with new AF at 105 to 110/min.
ddx.against: Afebrile (37.0 °C), alert and oriented, no vomiting, only mildly increased bowel frequency, no heart failure, haemodynamically stable. A Burch–Wartofsky score may reach the mid-20s to 30s from the AF and restlessness alone, but clinically she is compensated. Admit if fever, confusion, vomiting, worsening tachycardia or heart failure develop.

guide:
The source case is examination-led, so Part 1 should be a brief focused history (about 3 minutes) and then a full thyroid examination. The examiner gives findings from the Exam findings only when the candidate says what they examine, and gives the vital signs as stated when asked. Eliza gives the weight loss and other symptoms only when asked. The irregular pulse can be noted in Part 1, but atrial fibrillation is confirmed and marked from the ECG in Part 2.

In Part 2 hand over all three results together and ask the four questions in order. Questions 1 to 3 are a discussion with the endocrinology registrar and the examiner; for Question 4 Eliza is back in the room and asks her questions. Items 32 and 35 can be earned in Question 3 or 4. The source's question on other causes of thyrotoxicosis is answered in Question 2. Doses do not need to be exact; accept any beta blocker with a sensible dose and a plan to start carbimazole now or at an endocrinology review within days.

A high-performing candidate asks about pressure symptoms, eye symptoms including vision and diplopia, palpitations with cardiac red flags, causes, contraception and smoking. They examine the hands, tremor, reflexes, eyes from the front, side and above with lid lag and an H test, inspect the neck with a swallow and tongue protrusion, palpate from behind, percuss and auscultate, and check the legs. In Part 2 they call TSH-independent thyrotoxicosis, use the TRAb and clinical features to name Graves' disease with thyrotoxic AF, calculate CHA2DS2-VA, start a beta blocker, plan carbimazole with agranulocytosis counselling, refer to endocrinology and ophthalmology, and address smoking and pregnancy.

A borderline candidate palpates the neck without a swallow or skips the eyes, misses the irregular pulse, calls the results "hyperthyroid" without giving the cause, forgets anticoagulation assessment or agranulocytosis counselling, or gives vague safety netting.
explain:
The thyroid examination

Decide first whether you are looking for hyper- or hypothyroidism, and examine thyroid status as well as the gland. Seat the patient with the neck and arms exposed.

  • General: habitus, restlessness, clothing for the weather; vital signs, especially pulse rate and rhythm.
  • Hands and arms: warm moist skin, palmar erythema, onycholysis, thyroid acropachy (Graves'), fine tremor, brisk reflexes (slow-relaxing in hypothyroidism), Pemberton's sign (facial plethora with arms raised from a retrosternal goitre obstructing the thoracic inlet).
  • Eyes: exophthalmos from the front, side and above; lid retraction and lid lag; chemosis; eye movements with an H test for ophthalmoplegia and diplopia; acuity and colour vision if eye disease is present.
  • Neck: inspect for goitre, scars, redness and distended veins; a goitre rises on swallowing, a thyroglossal cyst rises on tongue protrusion. Palpate from behind for size, number of nodules, character, texture, tenderness, attachment and the lower border; check nodes and trachea. Percuss the manubrium for retrosternal extension and auscultate for a bruit.
  • Legs: pretibial myxoedema (Graves'), proximal myopathy, reflexes.

Graves' disease

TSH receptor antibodies stimulate the gland, giving a diffuse, smooth, vascular goitre (often with a bruit) and thyrotoxicosis. Orbitopathy, pretibial myxoedema and acropachy are specific to Graves'. Smoking increases the risk and severity of eye disease.

Interpreting the results

  • Suppressed TSH with high free T4 and T3 is TSH-independent thyrotoxicosis (Graves', toxic nodules, thyroiditis or exogenous hormone); a normal or high TSH would suggest a TSH-secreting pituitary tumour or thyroid hormone resistance.
  • Positive TRAb confirms Graves' disease, so a technetium scan is not needed. Scintigraphy helps when TRAb is negative: diffuse high uptake (Graves'), patchy uptake (toxic multinodular goitre), a single hot nodule (toxic adenoma), or low uptake (thyroiditis, exogenous thyroxine, iodine excess).
  • ECG: AF occurs in a minority of people with thyrotoxicosis, more often in older people; in a young woman without heart disease it is almost certainly thyroid-driven.
  • Baseline FBC and LFTs are checked before antithyroid drugs.

Other causes of thyrotoxicosis

Toxic multinodular goitre and toxic adenoma (nodular glands, usually older people); thyroiditis (subacute painful, painless, postpartum), where thyrotoxicosis comes from release of stored hormone and is often followed by a hypothyroid phase; amiodarone; iodine excess (contrast, kelp); and excess thyroxine (factitious or supplements).

Management (eTG)

  • Beta blocker for symptoms and rate control, e.g. propranolol 10 to 40 mg orally three or four times daily, unless asthma; a non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blocker is an alternative.
  • Carbimazole, commonly 15 to 30 mg daily to start, reduced as she becomes euthyroid; check free T4 and T3 every 4 to 6 weeks because TSH can stay suppressed for months. A 12 to 18 month course gives remission in about half; relapse is common.
  • Adverse effects: rash and itch are common; agranulocytosis is rare, usually in the first months, and presents with sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers; liver injury is rare. Carbimazole can harm the fetus in early pregnancy, so propylthiouracil is preferred in the first trimester under specialist care.
  • Radioiodine: not in pregnancy or breastfeeding; avoid pregnancy for at least 6 months afterwards; can worsen active orbitopathy, especially in smokers, and is avoided or given with steroid cover in active eye disease. Most people become hypothyroid and need lifelong thyroxine.
  • Total thyroidectomy: suits a large goitre, significant eye disease or a wish for pregnancy soon; risks hypocalcaemia and recurrent laryngeal nerve injury; lifelong thyroxine.

Thyrotoxic atrial fibrillation

Rate control with a beta blocker is first line; digoxin works poorly in thyrotoxicosis. Most patients revert to sinus rhythm within months of becoming euthyroid, so cardioversion is deferred until then. Stroke risk is assessed with CHA2DS2-VA as in other AF (Australian AF guideline): Eliza scores 0, so anticoagulation is not recommended; reassess if AF persists or risk changes, and anticoagulate around any planned cardioversion. Arrange an echocardiogram. Manage in ED if she is unstable, has chest pain or heart failure, or shows features of thyroid storm (fever, agitation or confusion, vomiting or diarrhoea, very fast heart rate). The Burch–Wartofsky score is sensitive but not specific: AF and restlessness alone can put a compensated patient like Eliza in the "impending storm" range, so it supports clinical judgement rather than replacing it.

Graves' orbitopathy

Refer to ophthalmology. Stop smoking, use lubricants and sunglasses, and sleep head-up. Selenium may help mild active disease (EUGOGO). Dysthyroid optic neuropathy (reduced acuity or colour vision) and corneal exposure are emergencies.

Safety netting

Stop carbimazole and get a same-day FBC for sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers. Call 000 for chest pain, breathlessness, fainting, a very fast heartbeat, stroke symptoms or fever with confusion. Same-day eye review for visual change, double vision or eye pain. Review in a week, TFTs in 4 to 6 weeks, with endocrinology and ophthalmology follow-up and contraception advice.

Her eyes: grittiness, redness and staring often improve as the thyroid settles, especially if she stops smoking; bulging may not fully resolve, and specialist treatment (including later surgery) is available if it persists.
points: Examine thyroid status as well as the gland: hands, tremor, reflexes, eyes from the front, side and above, the neck with a swallow and tongue protrusion, palpation from behind, percussion of the manubrium, a bruit, and the legs.

A suppressed TSH with high free T4 and T3 is TSH-independent thyrotoxicosis and does not by itself separate Graves' from toxic nodules, thyroiditis or exogenous hormone; positive TSH receptor antibodies confirm Graves' disease, and eye signs, pretibial myxoedema and acropachy are specific to it.
Thyrotoxic AF is rate-controlled with a beta blocker and usually reverts once euthyroid; decide on anticoagulation with CHA2DS2-VA as for any AF, and defer cardioversion until euthyroid.
Counsel everyone starting carbimazole: sore throat, fever or mouth ulcers mean stop the tablet and get a same-day full blood count.

Carbimazole and radioiodine both affect pregnancy: advise reliable contraception, plan pregnancy with endocrinology (propylthiouracil in the first trimester), and avoid pregnancy for at least 6 months after radioiodine.
Smoking worsens Graves' orbitopathy and radioiodine can aggravate it; reduced vision, altered colour vision or double vision need same-day eye review.
